title: UK to pay 'participation' fee to deliver EU deals
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The UK has agreed the deals in a bit to cut red tape for British companiesByPaul SeddonPolitical reporterThe
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The UK has agreed the deals in a bit to cut red tape for British companiesByPaul SeddonPolitical reporterThe UK will pay a "participation fee" to the EU as part of the deals agreed by Andy Burnham, according to legal documents.The surcharge will go towards the running costs of EU agencies and systems required to deliver two of the agreements unveiled by the prime minister last week.It will be paid in addition to a contribution towards costs that broadly mirrors how EU members contribute to the bloc's shared budget, the documents show.The government has sought to contrast the financial costs of the deals against their overall effect on the economy, which it estimates will receive an eventual boost by billions a year due to increased trade. The government is yet to publish an estimate of overall additional costs, but officials said they expected them to be in the low tens of millions per year and "massively outweighed" by predicted economic gains.British ministers had already said they were prepared to pay towards administrative costs required to implement deals to re-link the UK to the EU's carbon trading regime, and align Britain with the EU's food standards.Now, details of how the payments will be calculated have been revealed in treaties to deliver the two agreements, which are meant to take effect during 2028.Legal text for a third agreement agreed last week, on youth visas for 18 to 31 year olds, is expected to be published in the coming days. Fee detailsAccording to the treaties, the payments will be made as a share of the running costs of three EU agencies, as well as various systems that will be used to implement the food standards and emissions deals.The bulk of the payments, to be made in euros, will come in the form of an "operational contribution" in proportion to the size of the British economy compared to that of the EU.This broadly mirrors the way in which EU member states split the cost of their main contributions towards the bloc's overall budget.But in addition, the UK will also pay a "participation fee" set at 4% of its main contribution figure.The government has pointed to the 2021 Brexit trade agreement negotiated by the Conservatives, which also applied an additional surcharge to UK contributions towards the cost of relevant EU programmes.However, any additional contributions are likely to be seized upon by opponents of the latest deals.Ministers had declined to enter into specifics of the fees during negotiations on the treaties. On Sunday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the latest deals agreed by Burnham were "not about cost to the taxpayer". 'Extraordinary powers'It comes as the government published separate legislation granting it broad powers to incorporate new EU laws required to implement the agreements, without having to hold a full vote each time.The food standards deal in particular will mean Britain will have to align with scores of current EU food-related laws that have been updated since Brexit, along with future rules in these areas. The government argues the new powers are required because it would be impractical to run a full parliamentary process each time UK legislation needs to be updated to make the agreement work.But it has prompted criticism from opposition parties, because the UK no longer has voting rights at the EU to shape European legislation.The government argues the UK will get a say on new rules, with the treaty texts confirming British experts can be consulted when new EU laws are being drawn up, with the UK granted "observer" status in certain meetings.But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham was showing "disdain for the democratic process" by asking for a "blank cheque to install and enact EU law"."The prime minister is telling MPs to hand him extraordinary powers whilst having no idea what the EU will actually agree to," she added.Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has argued the Burnham's deals would take Britain back into "much of the European Union's single market".He added: "European economies are not growing as fast as ours. The idea that getting closer to the EU will mean growth for us is a myth."

schema.headline: UK to pay 'participation' fee to deliver EU deals

title: Zelensky tells BBC US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough
description: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying that delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives
body: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying that delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough during peace talks.In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president also said it was "strange" that Donald Trump had posted a picture of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend"."Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English."He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, suggesting it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during WWII.Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.He said talks were expected to resume in December.On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.The Kremlin appears to be resisting.In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Amercians were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems."It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said."The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.So whose decision was that?"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.He declined to be more specific.But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.They have also plunged much of the city into darkness."[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said."People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

schema.headline: Zelensky tells BBC US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough

title: Huw Edwards gives first interviews since child abuse image conviction
description: ByIan YoungsLucy Manning and Larissa KennellyDisgraced former BBC News presenter Huw Edwards has given his first interviews since being convicted in 2
body: ByIan YoungsLucy Manning and Larissa KennellyDisgraced former BBC News presenter Huw Edwards has given his first interviews since being convicted in 2024 for making indecent images of children.Edwards is seen saying he believes "silence is toxic" in a clip of a podcast released by the Observer newspaper, and he has also been interviewed for a Channel 4 documentary.Government minister Anna Turley told LBC, external she was "deeply uncomfortable" with the interviews, while shadow culture secretary Rebecca Paul said: "This man shouldn't get a minute of airtime". Channel 4 has defended the documentary. A spokesperson told the BBC that a "highly experienced director" holds Edwards to account with "no questions off limits, revealing his account of what led to his offending and very public downfall".Edwards, formerly the BBC's most senior news presenter, pleaded guilty in July 2024 to three counts of making indecent images of children and was given a suspended six-month prison sentence.During the court case, Edwards admitted having 41 images, which were sent to him on WhatsApp – including some showing a victim aged between seven and nine.In a trailer for the Channel 4 programme, director Patrick Forbes asks what he was doing, to which Edwards replies: "Oh, you want me to analyse what I was doing? I mean, seriously?"Asked again, he replies: "I'd lost the plot."The interviewer challenges him by saying: "Well, come on," to which Edwards angrily replies: "No, not come on."Despite that apparent combative stance, Edwards wrote on his blog on Thursday: "I want viewers to know that I did not avoid a single question, and that I answered each as honestly as I could, including those about deeply personal matters: my relationships, my temperament, my sexuality."Explaining his reasons for giving the interviews, he said: "My difficulties became front-page news, and the account that took hold was, in places, misleading or simply untrue."Those promoting false narratives are also, unsurprisingly, the ones questioning my right to set the record straight."I was left with a choice: to let that faulty account stand forever, or to offer my own."In a statement, Forbes said it was "an important film to make"."It's rare to find a subject that touches on so many significant contemporary issues – whether it's celebrity culture or the power of the media – as well as enduring questions about crime and punishment," he said.Channel 4's documentary, titled Huw Edwards - Guilty, will be broadcast on Tuesday.In the clip for his separate interview with the Observer and its Tortoise Investigates podcast, Edwards is seen saying: "Lots of the advice I've had is just be quiet, don't say anything."Interviewer Ceri Thomas, a former editor of the BBC's Today programme and Panorama, said he was "just deeply curious about how it was that a man of such prominence had got himself into this unbelievable, terrible fix".The interviews have been criticised by three people who previously spoke to BBC News about allegations of Edwards' inappropriate behaviour.One, who accused him in 2023 of sending them threatening messages, said it was "incredibly bizarre that anyone, big names like Channel Four, are platforming him when he's a convicted sex offender".The person, who is anonymous and not connected to the criminal case, told BBC News on Thursday that Edwards was "clearly trying to do a bit of damage repair" and they were "annoyed that he's being able to air these opinions".Another person, who said Edwards sent them suggestive and "pushy" messages when they were working at the BBC, and was also not involved in the court case, said: "I'm pretty disgusted they are giving him the air time."Additionally, a former junior BBC employee, who previously told BBC Newsnight's Victoria Derbyshire they had received inappropriate messages from Edwards, said "it seems a strange and irresponsible decision to give a platform to tell his story after the crimes he has been found guilty of."I hope that consideration has been given to his victims."Meanwhile, Rosamund Urwin, chief news correspondent for the Sunday Times, who jointly led the paper's 2023 investigation into Russell Brand, reacted to Thomas's statement by saying: "An 'unbelievable terrible fix' is quite the euphemism for someone viewing child abuse images of victims as young as 7."The podcast will be released on Tuesday. Tortoise Media, which owns the Observer, has a deal to make some podcasts available on BBC Sounds, but the BBC said the Huw Edwards series would not be among them.Channel 4 and the Observer said Edwards had received no payment for the interviews or had any editorial input.There has also been significant political reaction to the interviews.Speaking to Newsnight, Independent MP Rosie Duffield, who sits on the Women and Equalities Select Committee, said, "I'm just not sure why this was commissioned". "To know that hundreds of thousands of people are going to be watching it and sort of discussing it as though it's casual entertainment, I think personally, that is probably incredibly traumatic" to victims, she added.Senior Labour MP Anna Turley told LBC that "for too long, so many of these people in the public eye have been able to have a sort of free pass".Conservative culture spokeswoman Rebecca Paul shared a clip of Channel 4's Huw Edwards interview promo on X, writing: "Why on earth is a state-owned broadcaster platforming this depraved sex offender?"

schema.headline: Huw Edwards gives first interviews since child abuse image conviction

title: 'Horrible spike' in flu warning as hospital admissions surge
description: Speaking at the NHS Alliance autumn conference, Sir Jim said he was asked to wear a mask for the first time in years during a hospital visit, saying i
body: Speaking at the NHS Alliance autumn conference, Sir Jim said he was asked to wear a mask for the first time in years during a hospital visit, saying it was "a bit of a shock"."I think we have more beds occupied with flu than we did this time last year, as we're just about going to that horrible spike in flu," he said.According to the UKHSA, almost 9.5 million people under the age of 65 in clinical risk groups - including those with lung conditions, kidney or liver disease and diabetes - are eligible for the flu jab. However, only 34% had received a flu vaccine up to 22 November, leaving almost 7 million without vital protection.Sir Jim also condemned corridor care in hospitals saying that it had become "embedded" in some parts of the health service."It's not something any of us would want for our families, our mothers, our aunties, uncles – whether it's from a safety point of view, or more importantly from a personal dignity point of view," he said, adding there was a need to get a grip and eliminate it.Sir Ciaran Devane, chief executive of the NHS Alliance, representing employers, said: "While the flu season is clearly hitting earlier this year and could add to the strain on NHS services heading into another difficult winter, we are yet to see how or when it will peak."The NHS has already had to deal with the challenge of heatwaves this summer, so this could pile yet more pressure on already squeezed services."UKHSA flu lead Dr Suzanna McDonald urged people to get vaccinated, saying thousands of people die from the flu every year.Flu levels are expected to increase further as Christmas approaches and people start socialising indoors more.McDonald also called on those who are ill with respiratory symptoms to practise good hand hygiene by washing hands with warm soapy water, cough and sneeze into elbow or into a tissue, and to stay at home in bed and avoid anyone at much higher risk from catching diseases.Meanwhile, it emerged that just a little over a third of toddlers in England have had a vaccine so far this autumn on the NHS.Two and three-year-olds can have the vaccine, given as a nasal spray, for free at pharmacies.But the UKHSA said just 37% of those eligible had taken up the offer.School age children usually have the vaccine at school, with a catch-up available in pharmacies until 1 December for those who missed it.McDonald said: "Please don't dismiss the importance of a flu vaccine for your children."It will help keep them out of hospital and even save lives."This time last year an early increase in flu cases caused real concern across the NHS. The virus was spreading sooner than expected and the fear was that the numbers would continue climbing right through the always challenging Christmas and New Year period.  As it happened the outbreak peaked early and the bleakest predictions did not become reality.  This time hospital admissions with flu patients are a little higher than 12 months ago after another early surge materialised. Once again, officials do not know when the peak might be reached. Adding to the challenges is an increase over the last year in patient numbers with a range of illnesses and conditions, partly explained by the ageing population. That means even more pressure on hospitals and their staff. A bad flu winter could create significant problems.

schema.headline: 'Horrible spike' in flu warning as hospital admissions surge

title: Sandpapergate: Cricket Australia outlines terms of reference for independent hearing into scandal
description: Cricket Australia's fresh independent probe into the sandpapergate scandal has been widened to include the 2017-18 Ashes series against England.The te
body: Cricket Australia's fresh independent probe into the sandpapergate scandal has been widened to include the 2017-18 Ashes series against England.The terms of reference for the independent forum have been published and the scope will include "ball-management practices in the Australian men's team during the 2017–18 season", which includes the Ashes series Australia won 4-0.Also included are all four Tests of the subsequent South Africa tour and the investigation which followed when the ball-tampering scandal emerged.Cricket Australia has pledged to publish the full independent report and recommendations within 30 days of receiving them.All those involved in Australia's 2018 tour of South Africa will be invited to speak to the independent forum, though none will have to do so and no retrospective sanctions will be handed out.The scandal was reignited by the release of former batter Usman Khawaja's autobiography. In it, Khawaja claimed the entire team knew about ball-tampering in the third Test of their series against South Africa in Cape Town.The four frontline bowlers in that 2018 team - Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon and current Test captain Pat Cummins - have always denied knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper on the ball. Cummins has called Khawaja's recollection of events "nonsense".However, former team-mates David Warner and Cameron Bancroft - two of three players who were banned for their part in the scandal, alongside Steve Smith - have backed Khawaja's version of events."All participants in Australia's 2018 tour of South Africa, including players and support staff, will be invited to take part in the Independent Forum, as will CA management and directors at that time," Cricket Australia said."While all involved will be encouraged to participate, there will be no compulsion to do so. All materials supplied will be treated as confidential unless otherwise stated by the participant and no sanctions will be retrospectively applied."Participants can choose to attend the Independent Forum in person, online and/or provide information via written accounts or through relevant documents and materials."The forum will be open for six weeks."This is an opportunity to provide their accounts in a safe environment and to provide the CA Board with relevant information including about the events of that tour and resultant investigation," CA chair David Boon said."We are acutely aware of the enormous toll the renewed focus on this tour eight years ago has had on those involved and their welfare remains our main priority."This forum is the best opportunity for people to speak and be heard, and for CA to listen and learn."Publishing the report in full is part of our commitment to transparency, and to be open with cricket fans about what we learn."It is also very important to understand that it will not seek to sanction or recriminate."

schema.headline: Sandpapergate: Cricket Australia outlines terms of reference for independent hearing into scandal

title: Two Italians killed in strike in Kuwait, as Iran denies responsibility
description: Two Italian nationals have died following a strike on a facility in Kuwait which both countries have blamed on Iran.The pair were technicians working
body: Two Italian nationals have died following a strike on a facility in Kuwait which both countries have blamed on Iran.The pair were technicians working for German arms manufacturing company Rheinmetall, Italy's foreign ministry said.Iran has denied responsibility for the attack, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying the incident looked "suspicious" and that Tehran would work with Kuwait and Italy to "determine the cause".Kuwait's defence ministry said earlier that four people - the two Italians, a Kuwaiti national and Pakistani national - had been injured from falling shrapnel after a number of drones from Iran were detected and intercepted.It comes just over a week after Kuwait said it had repelled overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase which hosts US forces - the first strikes in more than two months on the country.Recent exchanges of fire between the US and Iran, and a deadlock in negotiations, have raised fears of a major escalation in the war. The conflict began when US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, with Iran retaliating by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.On Thursday, Araghchi said he had expressed condolences over the deaths in calls with his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts and that the incident looked like a "precooked recipe for war", without expanding further.Earlier, the country's armed forces spokesperson Abolfazl Shekarchi said "no military or offensive operations have been conducted" by Iran.Kuwait's Army said the latest attack was on a "vital site in the country" and was the result of "heinous Iranian aggression", while confirming the deaths of the two Italian nationals.Italy's foreign minister was quoted by Italian media as saying that investigations showed that the drone used in the attack was manufactured in Iran and that Iranian proxies were known to carry out attacks in the region."The Rheinmetall Group is in deep mourning," the German firm said in a statement confirming the deaths of two of its staff members."Two highly valued employees lost their lives while carrying out their professional duties, as they were providing technical support for air defence systems," it added."Protecting people in the country was a matter of profound importance to them."Company management and the workforce are devastated that our colleagues have now lost their lives."Italian media outlets have named the two individuals. One of the men was reported to be 36, while the other was 65 and nearing retirement.The men had been performing maintenance on systems used by the Kuwait Armed Forces, according to Italian press agency Ansa citing Italy's foreign ministry.Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on X: "On my own behalf and on behalf of the government, I express my deepest sympathy and offer my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families. "My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families."European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media: "We must step up pressure on Iran to end these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours and our partners in the Gulf."Today's events are a further reminder that security in the Gulf is a security issue for us all."

schema.headline: Two Italians killed in strike in Kuwait, as Iran denies responsibility

title: Med Emre: Diesel tanker carrying tonnes capsizes near Ibiza, killing one
description: An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.The Med E
body: An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service."There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X. Elena Delgado, maritime captain of Valencia, told news agency AFP that a small slick that had formed around the boat had "disappeared". "The situation is stabilised," she said, adding that further inspections would be carried out on Friday morning. Earlier, regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk, as had originally been reported. The vessel remains partially submerged.The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia. It is unclear what caused the sinking.The chemical tanker was en route from Algeciras, in southern Spain, to Barcelona in the north-east.

schema.headline: Med Emre: Diesel tanker carrying tonnes capsizes near Ibiza, killing one

title: Huntingdon knifeman told doctor psychosis drugs weren't working
description: Violent knifeman told doctor his psychosis drugs weren't working days before train attackFigure caption, Could the Huntingdon train attack have been p
body: Violent knifeman told doctor his psychosis drugs weren't working days before train attackFigure caption, Could the Huntingdon train attack have been prevented?ByDaniel SandfordUK correspondentHurtling along at more than 120mph, passengers on an East Coast Mainline train bound for London King's Cross found themselves caught up in one of the worst acts of violence on Britain's rail network in recent times.Anthony Williams stabbed 10 people in five minutes on board the train last November, near Huntingdon, in Cambridgeshire, leaving some seriously injured. On Thursday, a jury found him guilty of 14 counts of attempted murder.It has now emerged that, in the month before that attack, the knifeman had twice contacted his GP to say the anti-psychosis drugs he was taking for schizophrenia were not working.But he never saw a doctor and did not receive additional mental health treatment.Now his trial at Cambridge Crown Court is over, BBC News can also report his long history of violent criminality, revealed through old court transcripts we have obtained.It stretched back two decades. In his teens Williams robbed people at knife point, including on a train. Even after he had started his 25-hour rampage, culminating in the Huntingdon attack, there were potential opportunities to arrest him.'Sorry record' of previous convictionsWilliams, who was born Anthony Abiola Oluwatuyi in London in 1993, first arrived on the police radar aged 12, when he was excluded from school for arson after setting fire to the toilets.One acquaintance from the time - who would only speak on condition of anonymity - told BBC News Williams would "turn people's pockets inside out just because he wanted to". They said: "He was a thug who brought a knife to class."Over the next seven years, he was convicted of 14 further offences, including five thefts, three robberies, and two offences of possession of a knife.In October 2012, aged 19, he robbed two fellow teenagers of their smartphones at knife point on a train, warning them: "If you tell, I will come back and find you."Train attacker found guilty of all 14 counts of attempted murderHow the Huntingdon train attack unfolded - carriage by carriageImage source, British Transport PoliceImage caption, Williams with a knife in Ritzy barbers in Peterborough the night before the train attackWhen he was sentenced for that at Wood Green Crown Court to three and a half years detention in March 2013, the judge referred to his "sorry record of previous convictions".Williams' barrister, Victoria Kerly, told the court he had mental health problems, adding: "They are things that I have myself experienced with him and they do raise some concerns for me."Drug dealing and mental health issuesBy the time Williams appeared at St Albans Crown Court in February 2020 he was a crack cocaine and heroin addict, as well as a drug dealer.He had been arrested the previous year in possession of heroin, crack cocaine and cannabis, as well as a pair of scales and 12 "burner" phones. Asked about his drug dealing, he told police: "If I don't do it, not good things will happen to me."He was sentenced to four years in prison, where he was sectioned and held in a psychiatric hospital until his release.Upon release, he moved to Peterborough to live with his mother and stepfather. At this stage it is unclear exactly what mental health treatment he received there, but the BBC understands that, following last year's train attack, Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS Foundation Trust launched an internal review.On 30 September 2025 - a month before the Huntingdon attack - Williams contacted his GP online about what he described as his "deteriorating mental state", saying his drugs were not working.Figure caption, Footage of Williams' arrest and passengers fleeing was shown to the juryThe doctor told him he should be taking 200mg of the Quetiapine he had been prescribed to treat his paranoid schizophrenia, but he was only taking 100mg.The GP invited him to a meeting on 14 October which he did not attend. Williams contacted the doctor again on 23 October, again saying the medication was ineffective - but he did not respond when the GP tried to get back to him.In a phone call with a taxi firm on 31 October, the night before the train attack, Williams can be heard apparently speaking to voices in his head, saying things like "devil wanna play", and making strange noises, before then resuming the conversation normally.Following the attack, Williams told psychiatrists "things were bad" in the days before it."I was paranoid people were going to attack me. They were coming for me. I was hearing a lot of voices, feeling a lot of fear," he said. "I just needed to protect myself. It was me or them."Psychiatrists who assessed Williams after the attack concluded he had been "acutely psychotic".Dr Bernard Chin said Williams was suffering from "paranoid persecutory delusions" that he was the focus of "an organised conspiracy that came about because of the machinations of the devil".Following the guilty verdicts, NHS England's East of England division said it would commission an independent investigation into the healthcare provided to Williams "to help identify any opportunities for learning and improvement".Possible opportunities missed by policeImage source, British Transport PoliceImage caption, Anthony Williams taking a drink on the train in the middle of his attackA month before the Huntingdon attack, a man was attacked close to Williams' home.Two officers from Cambridgeshire Police now face a gross misconduct hearing over their handling of the alleged assault. The Independent Office for Police Conduct said one of the officers allegedly failed to conduct appropriate inquiries and both officers were alleged to have concealed this by falsely claiming no CCTV was available.Having been in and out of court for two decades, Williams, now 33, continued his violence before boarding the train.The day before the train attack, on 31 October, Williams carried out three knife attacks in Peterborough, injuring one person. None were recorded on CCTV.He then went into Ritzy's Barbers in the city, threatening those inside with a knife. That incident was caught on camera. It was reported to police two hours later, but officers did not collect the CCTV until three days later - two days after the Huntingdon train stabbings.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Forensic teams combed the train at Huntingdon station as part of a major investigationOn the morning of the Huntingdon attack, on 1 November, Williams stabbed a teenager on a Docklands Light Railway (DLR) train near Pontoon Dock station, in east London. British Transport Police (BTP) said initial CCTV of the attack was of poor quality.However, the force tracked the knifeman to nearby Poplar DLR station where officers obtained clearer CCTV images.Using reactive facial recognition software they generated a match with Williams, who had two addresses recorded on police systems - one in Waltham Cross, in Hertfordshire, the other in Peterborough.Officers prioritised the Waltham Cross address because there was a "recent financial trace" to it, and it was closer to the DLR attack.At 6:48pm that day, BTP officers turned up at the address to arrest Williams. But half an hour earlier, at 6:16pm, Williams had left his actual home - in Peterborough - to travel to the station and launch his stabbing spree on a London North Eastern Railway (LNER) train.BTP Deputy Chief Constable Stuart Cundy said "it was certainly not for want of trying by the officers who responded and commenced our investigation immediately after the attack on the train at Pontoon Dock".But when it comes to other incidents during Williams' chequered past, whether criminal or health-related, various authorities will now have to assess whether anything could have been done before he boarded that LNER train.Additional reporting by Robbie Kalus

schema.headline: Huntingdon knifeman told doctor psychosis drugs weren't working

title: Tebbutt attack in Lamu: Kenyan Ali Kololo says Met Police ruined his life
description: A Kenyan woodcutter who was wrongly sentenced to death over an attack on a British couple has told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Polic
body: A Kenyan woodcutter who was wrongly sentenced to death over an attack on a British couple has told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Police involved in the case destroyed his life.Somali gunmen broke into David and Judith Tebbutt's beach bungalow on the Kenyan coast in 2011. They shot David dead and abducted Judith, holding her captive in Somalia for six months.Met detectives flew to Kenya to assist the investigation. Their evidence helped convict Ali Kololo, who spent more than a decade in prison before his conviction was overturned.Kololo is suing the Met, claiming a senior officer, former Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, gave misleading evidence at his trial and acted unlawfully to secure his conviction.In his first media interview, he told the BBC about his 15-year ordeal and his fight for compensation, which the Met is challenging in court.We meet on Lamu, a small island off Kenya's northern coast, once a thriving Swahili port. People and goods are still carted through its narrow stone streets by donkey rather than car.It was here, in 2013, that Kololo was sentenced to death.Standing at the jetty, where police once brought him ashore in handcuffs, he relishes being free. But he is struggling to rebuild his life."Everything was taken from me. I'm starting from zero. I don't think I'll ever go back to who I was before," he says.Before his arrest, Kololo lived with his wife and their three young children. He had once worked as a groundskeeper at the resort where the Tebbutts were staying, but by 2011 he earned his living felling trees in a local forest and selling the wood."My life was very good," he says. "I was fending for myself, taking good care of my family."Within 24 hours of the attack, Kenyan police had arrested him."I was beaten with clubs and thrown into a car," he says. "They beat me for days, burning me with cigarettes, forcing me to confess to things. They subjected me to torture like no other."Kololo could not read or write. He says police made him put his thumbprint on a statement claiming he had led the attackers to the Tebbutts."I didn't understand anything," he says, calling the statement "a mountain of lies". "I signed it without knowing what it was because of the state they had put me in".The Kenyan police told us it "at all times strives to work within the law". Kololo is not suing them.Within days of the attack, a team of Met officers, led by then Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, arrived to support the Kenyan investigation. The UK government had instructed the officers not to accept information from the Kenyan authorities that had been obtained by interrogating detainees.But Hibberd requested Kololo's statement and later relied on it when giving evidence for the prosecution at his trial.In court, Hibberd also presented evidence linking Kololo to the attack. He told the Kenyan court Kololo had been wearing a type of shoe that matched footwear marks found in the sand at the resort. The officer who had arrested Kololo said he was barefoot when he was handed to police. Hibberd did not disclose that the Met's own forensic examination could not establish whether the shoe in question had made the marks.At the trial, Kololo did not initially have a lawyer. He had to cross-examine all the prosecution witnesses himself, including Hibberd, through an interpreter who spoke Swahili, which was not Kololo's first language."I believe I was framed because I am a poor man and I did not have the strength or means to fight for myself," Kololo says.Kololo was convicted of kidnap and robbery with violence - the only person ever convicted in connection with the attack. He spent three years on death row before his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.He recalls seeing his prison file. In the space for the expiry date, someone had written "death"."I was completely heartbroken. I believed I could be executed at any moment, and I would never see my family, my children, ever again."Years later, the UK's Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) established that Hibberd had omitted significant forensic evidence at the trial. It found that he would have had a case to answer for gross misconduct, but he could not face disciplinary proceedings because he had retired from the force. At the time, his lawyer said Hibberd absolutely disagreed with the report's findings.In April 2023, Kenya's High Court quashed Kololo's conviction, because of doubts over the prosecution's evidence. This followed years of work by the legal charity Reprieve and a Kenyan lawyer, Alfred Olaba, who represented him for free.They were supported by Judith Tebbutt, who believed Kololo was innocent. In an interview with the BBC in 2022, she said he had been scapegoated by Scotland Yard."He was not there on the night. He was not part of the group that held me. They've put this man in prison without any real evidence."More than three years after his release, Kololo says he is still living with the effects of his torture and decade in prison. As we walk the narrow streets of Lamu's old town, his thin frame moves stiffly. He is on edge. "My mind is not good," he says. "I have not recovered."He remembers being kept in a filthy, bedbug-ridden cell with up to eight other inmates, which he thought he would never leave. Twice he contracted tuberculosis and nearly died.Kololo is now too frail to do the woodcutting he once relied on to make a living. He tries to grow enough to eat on the land around his home, but erratic rain makes it difficult."I have nothing. On the days I get food, I eat, and on the days I don't, I endure."He lives alone in a mud hut. His wife divorced him after he went to prison, and their children went to live with his mother. They dropped out of school because the family could not pay the fees. Kololo says they were not allowed to visit him in prison. When he was released, they barely remembered him, especially his youngest."They were too young. Only now are they starting to regain the memory that 'this is our father who disappeared'," he says. "If it weren't for my mother, my children might have died."For much of our time together, Kololo is remarkably upbeat. He trusts that his lawyers and God will deliver him justice. But when we talk about the Met, his demeanour shifts."I am extremely angry with the police," he says. "I'm also angry with the Kenyan Police. They collaborated to incriminate me. What [Hibberd] said destroyed my entire life and my children's lives."The Met has not apologised to Kololo or admitted wrongdoing. The force is contesting his compensation claim, which his lawyers say could take years to resolve."These people falsely accused me. Do I not deserve something?" he asks.The Met told the BBC that neither they nor Hibberd wanted to comment on Kololo's claim, but it said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Kololo, Mrs Tebbutt, her family and all those who have been affected by this terrible crime. The Metropolitan Police remains committed to supporting the Kenyan authorities in any way that may be possible, in order to get justice for Mrs Tebbutt and her late husband."Preetha Gopalan, Reprieve's head of UK litigation, describes the Met's behaviour in Kololo's case as "egregious". "They've spent 10 years trying to evade accountability in every way possible, now dragging him through the courts," she says. "It's possible for them to do the right thing, but they are unwilling, and so this ordeal continues to haunt Kololo and his family.""Even if I get a billion shillings, I will never be the same," Kololo says. "But if I get the justice I deserve, I can help my children and take care of myself when I am an old man."

schema.headline: Tebbutt attack in Lamu: Kenyan Ali Kololo says Met Police ruined his life

title: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua: Paris Fury clarifies fighter did not have schizophrenia diagnosis
description: Paris Fury, the wife of Tyson Fury, says the boxer has never received a diagnosis of schizophrenia.In clips promoting the release of a forthcoming Net
body: Paris Fury, the wife of Tyson Fury, says the boxer has never received a diagnosis of schizophrenia.In clips promoting the release of a forthcoming Netflix documentary, the heavyweight fighter spoke of his mental health struggles in the months after he beat Wladimir Klitschko to become world champion in 2015.He detailed hearing voices in his head, and wife Paris said he had "mild schizophrenia" .Netflix has now edited the film before its release on Friday, 27 November.In a statement, Paris Fury said: "I want to clarify a statement I made in the original version of the Tyson Fury documentary."I recalled a conversation from many years ago when discussing Tyson's condition and I used the word 'schizophrenic'. While Tyson did show some symptoms associated with schizophrenia, he doesn't have this condition and has never received a diagnosis."She added: "Mental health is complex, and it isn't always easy to find the right words, especially when you're living it with someone you love. I'm so proud of Tyson for really opening up in this documentary and want to say thank you for all the support we've received as a family."A spokesperson for Netflix told BBC Sport: "Following new information shared by the family relating to Tyson's official mental health diagnosis, we have worked alongside them to update the documentary accordingly ahead of launch."It comes after the British Boxing Board of Control said it was looking into Fury's comments about his schizophrenia diagnosis but was "fairly confident" the British heavyweight would be cleared to fight Anthony Joshua next month.Fury, 38, is due to face Joshua at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December, with the ringwalk expected in the early hours of 12 December."We are in the process of dealing with the matter but if there are any medical issues we wouldn't let anyone box - it doesn't matter if it's Tyson Fury or not, it could be anybody," Robert Smith, the board's general secretary, told BBC Sport."I'm fairly confident he will be absolutely fine. We're dealing with it now and we'll have an answer very shortly."Under regulation 8.1(b) of the British Boxing Board of Control's 2026 rules and regulations, external, schizophrenia is among the conditions that "may preclude" a boxer from obtaining a first licence, while for an existing licence holder the board "may take such action as in its absolute discretion it sees fit".Smith would not say what the process would involve over the next few days, saying "it's a medical matter".He said all boxers on the card would undergo medical checks, adding: "If our doctors are satisfied he's fit to box, he will box."Originally, the documentary featured the Furys recalling his admission to hospital in June 2016 with a suspected heart attack.Doctors said he had suffered an anxiety attack. He was diagnosed with schizophrenia after he left hospital, according to the film.The NHS describes schizophrenia as a form of psychosis, and symptoms can include hallucinations, delusions and muddled thoughts and speech."Words can't explain the darkness I was in," Fury said.The heavyweight, who struggled with drug and alcohol addiction after beating Klitschko, says a Halloween night out in 2017 prompted him to return to training, calling that a "turning point" after being "embarrassed by how I looked".He went on to beat Deontay Wilder in 2020 to become world heavyweight champion for a second time.

schema.headline: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua: Paris Fury clarifies fighter did not have schizophrenia diagnosis

title: The young hikers finding friendship and fresh air offline
description: Image source, Mohannad NajjarImage caption, The wild landscape of Glencoe in Scotland is where Mohannad has found calmByPhilippa RoxbyHealth reporterA
body: Image source, Mohannad NajjarImage caption, The wild landscape of Glencoe in Scotland is where Mohannad has found calmByPhilippa RoxbyHealth reporterAfter years toiling all day at a desk as an aerospace engineer in Istanbul, 26-year-old Mohannad Najjar decided to swap his screen for a degree in nature and theology in Cambridge and a volunteering gig as a scout leader.He walks in the countryside every weekend and has hiked in wild locations in the Scottish Highlands, which he credits with helping him think clearly."I just want to see something that's untouched, to be in nature," he says. "When you come in from a hike or a walk, you just feel different."Najjar is one of a growing number of young hikers in the UK. Nearly 9% of 16-34 year-olds are regular hill walkers or hikers, according to Sport England, up from 2.3% eight years ago.Figure caption, Watch: Why we're swapping screens for sceneryMany young walkers' groups from Inverness to Nottinghamshire have seen their membership rise over the past two years, according to the Ramblers walking charity. Demand has nearly doubled for a course it offers teaching map and compass skills to 18-25 year-olds.Many who sign up want to ditch their phones and no longer rely on a blue dot to navigate, says Alistair Cooper, who leads the Out There Award programme."There's a cohort that missed out on outdoorsy, fun stuff during Covid. They want to get out and explore - but often don't know where to start."Some 83% of people in the UK live in towns and cities, according to the UN, where research suggests noise, traffic, stress and information overload put huge demands on our brains, affecting our mental health."Nature is the environment we are adapted to, and being close to it brings benefits such as improved wellbeing, brain function and physical performance," says Dr Danny Longman, lecturer in human evolutionary physiology from Loughborough University."There is a theory that simply paying attention to trees and leaves allows our brains to recover," he says.Image source, Deborah OdutayoImage caption, For Deborah Odutayo, her navigation skills are now one of her biggest achievements'Grounding'Environmental science student Deborah Odutayo, 24, described going through "an identity crisis". "I didn't see myself as someone who works behind a desk from 9 to 5," she said.After solo travelling, Odutayo had dreams of living abroad but didn't know how to finance them. So she decided to change her mindset. "I just need to be outside, essentially. That's how I started like doing solo hikes and stuff. It feels very therapeutic - mostly for my mental health."She's since hiked in Kent and the Peak District, among other locations, and camped with an outdoor group in Dorset.Learning how to get around without using her phone or digital maps is something she is proud of, saying it feels "more intentional and grounding".Image source, Miranda Chambers-ReidImage caption, No matter the weather, Miranda Chambers-Reid gets outside any time she canFriendship fluxWalking gives people "an instant friend group" when life is in flux, says Miranda Chambers-Reid, who leads a Ramblers' walking group for people in their 20s and 30s in Sheffield."They don't want all of their friends to be work friends or old uni friends," she says.As a mum of a seven-year-old, she made a similar decision when she joined: "I thought, I don't want all of my friends to be mum friends."Over the last two years, the group has increased from 250 members to 350.For some it's more about a sense of achievement says Chambers-Reid, who herself covers about 30 miles of walking a week."I work in an office and I can't see the sky so whenever possible I will be outside."For Sej Chauhan, 27, her walking group is about making connections while keeping costs down."There's a growing interest in socialising in ways that don't involve drinking alcohol or spending lots of money," she says.Chauhan set up Girls Who Walk in her home town of Leicester after a lonely year spent studying in Bristol.To make that experience easier for others, the group's focus is on walking in parks, talking and female companionship. And there's always a stop for coffee. In two years, the group has grown to more than 300 members - most are 25-35 years old."There's no pressure, no barriers with walking," Chauhan says. "Social media can often fill the void outside of work and home, but it doesn't provide the connection that people are craving."Image source, Sej ChauhanImage caption, Walking together in Leicester's Victoria Park - the Girls Who Walk groupNot everyone can access green space easily or has the time to go hiking because of work or childcare commitments.Here are Longman's tips for getting your nature fix as close as possible to home:Move in nature - an urban park or garden will doListen to the sounds of the elements, like wind, rain, birdsongSmell the distinctive scent of pine forests, breathe in the outdoorsIf you are indoors, bring the sounds and imagery of nature into your home using apps

schema.headline: The young hikers finding friendship and fresh air offline

title: Bournemouth 'dreaming' of winning Europa League after beating Celta Vigo
description: Bournemouth are dreaming of winning the Europa League after staging a 10-man fightback to join a select band of teams to win their first five European
body: Bournemouth are dreaming of winning the Europa League after staging a 10-man fightback to join a select band of teams to win their first five European games.The Cherries trailed 1-0 to Iago Aspas' goal at Celta Vigo, and then went down to 10 men midway through the first half when Bafode Diakite was sent off.But second-half goals from Alvaro Rodriguez and Rayan gave the Cherries a 10th consecutive win in all competitions, extending their club record run.Bournemouth are only the third side to win each of their first five European matches (excluding qualifiers and including the Inter-Cities Fairs Cup), after Nuremberg in 1961-62 and Ararat in 1972-73.They top this season's table as the only club to win five out of five - and are closing in on a top-eight spot, which would mean they skip a play-off round and go straight into the last 16.Some fans have told the BBC they have already booked hotels in Frankfurt for the final on 26 May.As supporters sang about reaching that game, midfielder Alex Scott was asked for his thoughts on TNT Sports."Of course that's our dream. When you grow up wanting to be a footballer you dream of winning trophies," Scott said."Where this club has come from to where it is now, full credit to everyone who has built it."For players, it's a dream to be on the pitch playing for this club. We have still got wins to get to qualify into the top eight, and from there all focus is on pushing forward and hopefully we can go on and win it."The Cherries are in unprecedented times, with their biggest trophy to date being when they won the second-tier Championship in 2014-15.In terms of cups, they won the 1983–84 Associate Members' Cup - which later became the EFL Trophy.Head coach Marco Rose, who replaced Andoni Iraola in the summer, said: "It's always allowed to dream."If you get a competition like this you want to achieve the best possible thing. We know it's far away to go. Many games. Now it's about getting into the top eight to avoid more games and then we can see step by step."As well as just winning their games, Bournemouth are firing in the goals. They have netted at least twice in each match during this 10-game winning run.And they are the first side to score at least twice in each of their first five matches in Europe since Queens Park Rangers in 1976.The win on Thursday was made even more impressive by the fact they contested 75% of the game with 10 men.It came days after Manchester United seemed to implode after an early red card against Liverpool, losing 4-0.Former England manager Glenn Hoddle said on TNT: "They have deserved this result. They've played beautifully with 10 men - probably as good as I've seen a team play defensively and with the ball."I've not seen a team go down to 10 men for so long and dictate a game and deserve to win the game. They were absolutely brilliant."Cherries boss Rose told BBC Radio Solent: "What a team, what a spirit, what an energy."I said to Ty [Tyler Adams] sometimes it's not about tactics and formations and stuff like this. [David] Brooks did a great job when we got one player less - he played right defender like he played it for 10 years. We changed in the right moment. Everyone did his job on a really high level."We were just relentless and we never stopped to believe in this win and that's why big, big, big congratulations to the team. "You feel if you're one player down that it's a difficult night, but to handle a difficult night like this, it just shows the character of the team and of the whole group."The coach's belief in what they are doing filters through to the players.Amine Adli, who set up the equaliser, told the BBC: "At half-time, everyone still believed we can turn the game in our way and this is what happened."Everyone was like 'guys we can make it, we have to believe. If we score the game can change.'"Earlier this month, the attacking midfielder said he saw a lot of similarities to the Bayer Leverkusen team he was part of in 2023-24.That is not a bad comparison, considering they went unbeaten to win the domestic double, as well as reaching the Europa League final.So who can blame the Cherries for dreaming?

schema.headline: Bournemouth 'dreaming' of winning Europa League after beating Celta Vigo

title: I spend £200 a month on fancy meals by myself - would you dine solo?
description: Image source, Catherine SmithImage caption, Self-confessed foodie Catherine says the sense of freedom she gets from picking where and when she eats is
body: Image source, Catherine SmithImage caption, Self-confessed foodie Catherine says the sense of freedom she gets from picking where and when she eats is "empowering"ByEmily DoughtyCatherine Smith is perusing the menu at a high-end Mediterranean restaurant she has been excited to try. She has a new outfit on, and as she sips her rosé, she looks across at the empty seat - bliss."I think what is so special about solo dining is that you don't have to wait for people to make those plans. You can go out and do them yourself," says the 23-year-old.The self-confessed foodie is part of a growing trend of people booking tables for one - not because they're away with work but as a treat.As food trends analyst Charles Banks puts it: "[Eating alone] is becoming an intentional act, a little pocket of independence, indulgence and self-care."We spoke to solo dining fans and hospitality industry experts about how the trend is shaping the restaurant experience and asked if you would book a table for one.Figure caption, Solo dining: Would you book a table for one?Catherine, from Yorkshire, began dining solo at university and now does it at least once a month, choosing high-end restaurants she would not usually go to with friends and family.She has been to a range of places both in the UK and abroad, doing "lots of research" to find new spots, typically spending £100 to £200 per meal. "I think because a lot of my friends are vegan or vegetarian, I find that difficult sometimes because I'm quite a big meat eater," she says."I find it nice to be able to go out and pick a restaurant where I haven't had to scour through the menu to make sure that it's suitable for them."Catherine says the sense of freedom she gets from picking where and when she eats "feels empowering"."It definitely feels like not only a form of self-care but also a form of female liberation."Image source, Catherine SmithImage caption, While solo dining Catherine likes to read, journal or simply enjoy the peace and quiet Online booking platform OpenTable says it covers more than 5,000 restaurants in the UK. It says solo dining makes up the smallest proportion of its bookings in the UK but it is the fastest-growing category. Figures from 1 January to 31 August this year saw a rise of 23% in solo bookings compared to the same time period a year ago. It did not provide the data to the BBC to verify.Nishi Singh was an avid solo diner when she lived in London, but found it wasn't widely accepted after moving to Delhi."Someone approached me and said that they assumed I'd been stood up," she tells BBC World Service's The Food Chain podcast."It sparked a conversation about the culture around solo dining in Delhi and I was really shocked to hear that it's not really something people do."A couple of days later, she started documenting her solo dining experience on social media."Quite a lot of people have reached out and said that this is something they'd like to do and they're too scared to do it themselves," she says.The Food ChainRuth Alexander hears from solo diners - some who find peace and joy in a table for one, and others who would much rather not be aloneBanks, joint managing director of The Food People, a food trends and ideas agency, says that while solo dining isn't a "new consumer behaviour", changes in society mean it has become "almost aspirational".But he notes that not every restaurant has welcomed the trend. "A single diner could therefore feel like an inefficient use of a table rather than a customer the restaurant actively wanted."SoloTable, a website that helps identify restaurants suitable for solo diners, found that one in eight of 178 restaurants it surveyed in London did not accept online reservations from solo diners.Catherine says she has previously been turned away. "There are a lot of restaurants that I've wanted to go to before where they don't actually allow solo diners. And I've always found that to be really disappointing."Image source, Yousaf KhalidImage caption, Yousaf thinks solo diners could produce another useful business stream for restaurants However, some restaurants like Jungli, an Indian restaurant in Newcastle upon Tyne, is working to attract solo diners.Co-founder and director Yousaf Khalid has included high tables and bar seats in his recently opened restaurant. They also have charging points for laptops and phones."We want people to feel comfortable in these sorts of environments, being able to walk in on their own," he says.He has hired staff with "bigger personalities" to engage customers in conversation but they also know when to leave diners alone if they want a more solitary experience. Catherine urges anyone who fancies solo dining to give it a go."Food is a great way to bring people together, but it's also a great way to have good experiences on your own."I think with time, people will see and will start to accept it as something that's more normal."Additional reporting by Jemma Crew and Emma Jackson.Image caption, The Food Chain examines the business, science and cultural significance of food, and what it takes to put food on your plate. Listen to The Food Chain on BBC Sounds

schema.headline: I spend £200 a month on fancy meals by myself - would you dine solo?

title: UK net migration at lowest level since 1997 as asylum claims also fall
description: Net migration to the UK has fallen to 77,000 in the year to the end of June - the lowest level this century, other than during the pandemic, Office fo
body: Net migration to the UK has fallen to 77,000 in the year to the end of June - the lowest level this century, other than during the pandemic, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures show.Excluding the limited movements of people during the worldwide travel restrictions in 2020, the figures show the number of people arriving in the UK, minus those leaving, tumbled 92% from the record high of 944,000 in the year to March 2023.The ONS said this was the lowest net migration since 1997.Net migration is a measure of how many extra people are added  to the population in a given year.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures showed there was now "a sufficient degree of control" over the migration system.The prime minister went on to say: "I'm not going to say all of the work is done, and I don't want to appear complacent, but I think we're finally as a country getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see."The underlying official statistics show that an estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated.Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the figures showed that Labour had "delivered" after Conservative failures - but Chris Philp, her Tory shadow, said restrictions introduced by his party before the 2024 General Election were behind the falls.The 77,000 figure is also the first time the UK has seen net migration in the tens of thousands since former PM David Cameron's controversial pledge 16 years ago to reach such a level.The biggest factors in Thursday's record low were falls in the arrivals of people coming from outside Europe in three major categories of migration: The number of people coming to the UK to work fell by 45,000, asylum claims fell by 19,000 and the total number of students fell by 33,000.These number had been expected to fall because of the tightening of visas rules that began under the previous Conservative government which was then continued by Labour from July 2024.The effect of those policies, plus emigration from the UK, has meant that while net migration had already begun to fall, it more than halved in the last 12 months alone.Mahmood said the figures showed the government had "restored control"."We have brought net migration to 77,000, down 92% from its peak under the Conservatives," she said. "Where they failed, we have delivered for the British people."This is a reference to the so-called "Boriswave" after Brexit. When the UK left the EU and its freedom of movement rules, Boris Johnson's government allowed in many more people to work and study from other parts of the world.That led to the record-breaking arrivals in the year to March 2023. Johnson's successor, Rishi Sunak, introduced major restrictions on visas in the last months of his government.Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the falls were a result of those changes.In a post on X, he called for an "annual legally binding inward migration cap, set by Parliament, at far lower levels".Dr Ben Brindle of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, an impartial expert body, said: "We are entering an unusual period where immigration has come down and may still have further to fall - but we still have relatively high emigration, at least for the time being."Most of those emigrants are non-citizens, including people who arrived a few years ago when immigration was very high. That could push the net migration figures down even further next year, but the downwards blip is unlikely to last forever."In the year to June some 73,000 people arriving in the UK seeking asylum - down from 93,000 the previous year.As of September, the number of people who were waiting for a decision was 41,000, down 49% on the previous year.The Home Office said that these changes were driven by speeding up the system in taking decisions and a fall in the arrivals of new claimants via  "illegal entry routes" - largely meaning English Channel small boats.As a result, the number of people accommodated in September by the Home Office was 93,000 - 16% lower than the year before. Some 52 hotels that had been dedicated to asylum seekers have been emptied this year. While some 140 are still in use the total number of people in hotels has fallen 64% to 13,000.Responding to the latest statistics, Reform UK's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said the figures were "no cause for celebration"."This population explosion is why British people struggle to get a GP appointment, can't get housing and our prisons are overwhelmed."Liberal Democrat asylum and immigration spokesperson Paul Kohler said: "Britain faces serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services."A spokesperson for the Green Party added: "Creating a harsh environment for migrants and people seeking asylum is not a measure of success. The British people are overwhelmingly compassionate and will not be taken in by the dangerous and opportunistic narratives of the far right."

schema.headline: UK net migration at lowest level since 1997 as asylum claims also fall

title: Nearly 100 Labour MPs including ministerial aides oppose Rosebank oil field
description: Ministerial aides are among nearly 100 Labour MPs who have signed a letter to the prime minister to express their opposition to the Rosebank oil field
body: Ministerial aides are among nearly 100 Labour MPs who have signed a letter to the prime minister to express their opposition to the Rosebank oil field.The government could also face resignations from junior ranks if the project goes ahead, the BBC has been told.Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is due to make a decision on whether to give the go-ahead for drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland within weeks.The government has remained tight-lipped - both publicly and privately - about what it is likely to do.Those close to the energy secretary insist that she has not yet made her decision.But 92 Labour MPs have signed a letter, sent to the prime minister today, urging him not to allow the project to go ahead. Ministerial aides - the most junior rank of government - are among the signatures.The MP who organised the letter, Catherine Fookes, said: "If Rosebank is approved, champagne corks will pop in the offices of oil companies - but it will not make an iota of difference to my constituents' energy bills. "The oil belongs to private companies, and will only be shipped overseas to the highest bidder."What it will do, however, is accelerate the climate crisis, which is already pushing up food bills, causing devastating winter floods like those we saw in Monmouthshire last year, and fuelling wildfires across our green landscapes in summer."It's the most visible demonstration yet of the deep divides in the Labour Party over the issue.The decision about whether to approve Rosebank involves a legal process which technically lies solely with the energy secretary.Fahnbulleh has, in the past, been regarded as someone personally opposed to the oil field.Others in the cabinet, including Chancellor John Healey, have let it be known that they would like to see the project given the go-ahead; while the prime minister has repeatedly said he wants to take a "pragmatic" approach to North Sea oil and gas.But Fahnbulleh insisted last month that she alone would make the final decision and claimed the courts would ultimately side with her if colleagues attempted to overrule her.Influential pro-Rosebank voices suggested that senior ministers had toned down vocal support as the decision draws closer.They suggested this wasn't a sign that Rosebank would be vetoed, but because any obvious attempts to pressure the energy secretary might mean her final decision would be subject to a legal challenge. A number of MPs say they have heard conflicting claims - with both outcomes being predicted.What is clearer is that the government's decision will be controversial, whichever way it goes. There is a private and public battle playing out.Backers of the scheme argue approving it would provide an economic boost. The Conservatives also say it would enhance energy security.But oil is traded internationally – and the energy secretary has said approving the scheme will not help with immediate cost of living pressures. Rosebank would also be more polluting than Jackdaw, a gas field, which was approved last month.A fortnight ago, backers of the field were confident it would be approved.They believed the chancellor's language on energy bills at the Budget, coupled with the lack of political jeopardy that materialised from the approval of the Jackdaw gas field, had made their case stronger.The same group of MPs believe it would be difficult to reject Rosebank around the same time the prime minister is set to deliver a 10-year plan focused on reindustrialisation.The government has said oil and gas would be part of the energy mix for many years to come and sources in the trade union movement have suggested that if Rosebank doesn't go ahead, existing inward investment in the North Sea would be put at risk.While Labour's manifesto upon entering power in 2024 pledged not to "issue new licences to explore new fields", it does pledge to honour existing ones.In 2023, the then Conservative UK government granted a licence for Rosebank and a legal challenge followed.The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that the government had made the approval unlawfully, leaving the current Labour government to make a new decision on whether to give the go-ahead.The mood among some pro-Rosebank MPs changed this week, with several who back approval telling the BBC they were now worried it would be blocked.The BBC has spoken privately to Labour MPs involved in the debate, before the letter was sent to the prime minister, to get a sense of how divisive it is proving.One ministerial aide said: "There are quite a few of us who are considering our positions. I'm in that group. We want to see leadership on climate change."Another aide who said they might quit added: "There a group of us for whom we became Labour MPs because of climate change. It is the issue that motivated us into politics."Other aides – known in Westminster as parliamentary private secretaries – told the BBC they were opposed, but would stay in their jobs if it went ahead.Another said they thought there were increasing signs the prime minister would not be able to carry his party with him if the scheme was given the thumbs up.And another said the energy secretary might have to resign if it goes ahead, given her scepticism about the project.It has been reported in recent weeks that members of her team are encouraging opponents to make their feelings known. The BBC has been told the same.One MP, who backs Rosebank, said the behind-the-scenes operation had been so effective, the scheme was up in the air again.That has led to some anger at the energy secretary. One minister says: "Miatta has boxed herself in with how she's handled Rosebank. It's outrageous if she's encouraging MPs to speak up over Rosebank. We should get on and do it."Like the decision itself, the exact timeframe is unclear. But some opposition figures expect it mid-December.Whatever happens, it will be controversial and has already exposed splits in the Labour Party.

schema.headline: Nearly 100 Labour MPs including ministerial aides oppose Rosebank oil field
